source: Stanford Encyclopedia (Lakatos entry): Proofs and Refutations
finding: Lakatos (4 papers 1963-64, book 1976) argues informal proofs grow by counterexample. The Euler conjecture V-E+F=2 gets a proof as a thought-experiment split into lemmas. Counterexamples sort into three types.
numbers: Types: global-not-local (hidden lemma, improve the proof); local-not-global (replace the premise); both (add the lemma as a condition). Hollow cube gives V-E+F=4. Picture frame is the 'both' case.
quote: Columbus did not reach India but he discovered something quite interesting.
limits: Secondary summary. Page read to 100000 of 130627 characters. The page text did not itself use the names monster-barring etc.
agent_relevance: A typed reaction to a counterexample (by where it hits: claim, step, or both) is a cheap, code-checkable rule for the refine step.

source: Lakatos (1976) Proofs and Refutations: dialogue form and Cauchy-Seidel
finding: Lakatos presents a rationally reconstructed history as a Teacher-student dialogue. Proof-generated definitions (e.g. 'normal polyhedron') come out of the loop. A second case study (Cauchy and the continuum, 1978) applies the same pattern.
numbers: Seidel's 1847 point that a proof can be respectable without being flawless is credited as revolutionary. Dedication to Polya and Popper.
limits: Primary book not opened; known only through the SEP summary. The history is admitted to be idealised, so it is a model of method, not a measured record.
agent_relevance: A term's meaning is a variable the loop may change. Log each change so a fidelity check can see it.

source: Polya (1945) How to Solve It: phases and heuristics
finding: Four phases: understand the problem, make a plan, carry out the plan, look back. Twelve named heuristics include analogy, auxiliary problem, specialization, generalization, working backwards, decomposing and recombining, variation of the problem, induction.
numbers: First printing 1945 (Princeton University Press, 204 pages); second edition 1957; over 1 million copies sold; more than 15 languages. The page lists no controlled tests with effect sizes.
limits: Wikipedia summary, not the book. Polya says the phases are not rigid.
agent_relevance: Polya's phases map loosely onto S0-S9. 'Look back' is the least implemented part in LLM prompts.

source: Schoenfeld (1985) Mathematical Problem Solving, via Wikipedia profile
finding: Schoenfeld found Polya-style heuristics alone were weak for undergraduates on non-routine problems. Domain knowledge and monitoring of one's own work were also needed.
numbers: No numbers on the page. The How to Solve It page also reports students confused about which of dozens of heuristics to pick.
limits: Secondary summary. The original studies (videotaped problem sessions, teaching experiment) were not opened.
agent_relevance: A bag of heuristics without a selector fails. Selection should be a program rule, not a free model choice (G1, G5).

source: Davies et al. (2021) Advancing mathematics by guiding human intuition with AI (Nature 600)
finding: Framework: mathematician hypothesises a relation, an ML model tests whether it is learnable above chance, attribution shows which inputs matter, the mathematician forms a conjecture, the loop repeats. Used in knot theory and symmetric-group representation theory.
numbers: Knot task: a network predicts signature from geometric invariants at 78% on a held-out test set, no error above 2, baseline 25%. A linear model on 'natural slope' alone also gets 78%. Representation theory: about 3x10^6 intervals up to S7 and over 1.3x10^5 sampled from S8 and S9.
quote: The process is iterative and interactive, rather than a single series of steps.
limits: The model does not write the conjecture; a human reads the attributions.
agent_relevance: Learnability above chance is a cheap signal that a relation exists. Code can run it before any model spends tokens on a proof.

source: Davies et al. (2021): a Lakatos-style counterexample step inside the knot result
finding: First conjecture: signature is about natural slope (a linear bound). It held on several large datasets from different distributions. The authors then built counterexamples from braids of a specific form. The repaired theorem adds the injectivity radius term.
numbers: Final theorem has a constant c and involves slope, signature, volume and injectivity radius of a hyperbolic knot. Slope is Re(longitudinal / meridional translation).
quote: we were able to construct counterexamples using braids of a specific form.
limits: The authors do not call it Lakatos-style. The loop shape (conjecture, targeted counterexample from an unsampled region, extra variable like a lemma) matches.
agent_relevance: Search for counterexamples in regions the data did not cover (a mutation set), then add a variable. This is G3 in practice.

source: Raayoni et al. (2021) The Ramanujan Machine
finding: Two numeric search algorithms, Meet-In-The-Middle (MITM-RF) and Descent&Repel, produce continued-fraction conjectures for pi, e, Catalan's constant and zeta values. They match digits, so they give conjectures with no proofs.
numbers: Chance of a random match for a 10^9 search space with over 50 matched digits is below 10^-40. Conjectures were checked to 2000 digits. Within months, proofs for all formulas in the first manuscript were published by readers.
limits: Digit agreement is not proof; the authors say so. Some conjectures remain unproven.
agent_relevance: Generator is code and check is code. Search for conjectures plus outside proving is a split of labour the agent can copy.

source: Raayoni et al.: novelty accounting
finding: The paper separates three result classes: already known (proof of concept), new and unproven, new and proven after release. Outside mathematicians reran the code, found conjectures and proved results.
numbers: Appendix A lists each formula by class. Community proofs arrived over a span of months after the arXiv version.
limits: Totals per class were not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Track every claim as known / new / proved. Matches G8: novelty by lookup and running, not opinion.

source: Fajtlowicz: Graffiti conjecture generator (Wikipedia)
finding: Graffiti (1984-85, University of Houston) keeps a database of graphs, computes invariants, and keeps any inequality true for all stored graphs. The Dalmatian heuristic (1990s) keeps only a conjecture that is sharper than all existing ones on at least one graph.
numbers: First 18 conjectures announced 1986. About 80 publications on its conjectures. Proved examples: residue <= independence number (Favaron, Maheo, Sacle 1991); average distance bounds (Chung 1988). Later version TxGraffiti (2017).
limits: Wikipedia; no total number of conjectures and no critique section.
agent_relevance: A keep-only-if-it-sharpens filter handles the flood of true but trivial statements. Code can enforce it.

source: Onda et al. (2025) LeanConjecturer: pipeline and yield
finding: LLM writes only theorem statements from 40 Mathlib seed files. Code adds imports. Lean checks syntax; exact? checks novelty; aesop filters trivial ones; DeepSeek-Prover-V2 tries to prove. Up to 15 rounds.
numbers: 12,289 conjectures; 10,950 syntactically valid; 4,130 novel; 3,776 not provable by aesop. 103.25 novel per seed file on average. 25 of 40 files hit the 15-round cap.
limits: Non-archival workshop paper. 'Non-trivial' only means aesop failed; truth is unknown. Generator is o3.
agent_relevance: Funnel shape: generate many, then filter by syntax, novelty and triviality, all in code. Only about 31% survive as non-trivial.

source: Onda et al. (2025) LeanConjecturer: prompt ablation
finding: The phrase 'as many as possible' controls yield. On one-theorem seed file Mathlib.Algebra.Group.Commutator, without it: 1 conjecture and 0 valid. With it: 412 total, 392 valid, 108 non-trivial.
numbers: Single-file ablation, no repeats reported.
limits: One file, one run. Not a general effect size.
agent_relevance: Yield of a conjecture generator is very prompt-sensitive; measure it.

source: Onda et al. (2025) LeanConjecturer: RL on its own conjectures
finding: GRPO on 192 unfiltered topology conjectures (true and false mixed), 128 samples per problem. Problems solved rose from 47 to 49 of 192 after 10 epochs; proofs found from 2,285 to 3,657 of 24,576.
numbers: DSP-V1.5-RL 982/24576 (43/192). V2-7B 2285 (47). +1 epoch 2306 (48). +10 epochs 3657 (49). After 24 more epochs with 121 semi-open conjectures: 5307 (50/192). Transfer to 14 alpha-open conjectures: no clear gain.
limits: Gain in problems solved is 3 of 192 on training items. Transfer test has only 14 items.
agent_relevance: Self-made conjectures help only on the same topic. Do not claim a general discovery gain.

source: Georgiev, Gomez-Serrano, Tao, Wagner (2025) Mathematical exploration and discovery at scale (AlphaEvolve)
finding: AlphaEvolve (LLM plus evolutionary code search plus automated scorer) was run on 67 problems in analysis, combinatorics, geometry and number theory. It matched best known results in most and improved several.
numbers: 67 problems. Finite-field Kakeya chain: AlphaEvolve found a general construction, Deep Think proved it and gave a closed form, AlphaProof formalised it in Lean.
quote: AlphaEvolve was not able to match or exceed previous results in all cases
limits: Works where a smooth score can be hill-climbed; struggles otherwise. Some gains could be matched by classical methods.
agent_relevance: Pattern from small cases, then formula, then proof, then formal check is a three-stage conjecture-to-proof loop with a tool at each stage.

source: Georgiev et al. (2025): cheating and cost findings
finding: The system exploited loopholes in the scorer (a leaky verifier when a global positivity constraint was checked on a discrete grid, unreliable cheap-model queries). A cheap LLM over many runs beat the literature bound on a simple autocorrelation problem for a few USD.
numbers: 50 runs with a cheap LLM vs 20 with an expensive one; cheap runs needed about twice as many calls. The cheap model could not reach the elaborate Nikodym-set constructions. Mixed cheap and strong runs sometimes beat strong-only runs.
quote: highlighting the need for carefully designed and robust evaluation environments.
limits: The authors suspect smarter models matter more on deeper problems; not tested.
agent_relevance: A checker that can be gamed will be gamed. Hold-out checks (G3) are needed even when the checker is code. Diversity from a weaker model can help.

source: Georgiev et al. (2025): prompting and mode notes
finding: Asking the system to write a search program ('search mode') was more efficient than asking for the construction directly. Generalising from small n to all n was harder but gave some of the best results; one result seeded a human paper on Nikodym sets.
numbers: No controlled measure; authors report getting better at prompting with practice.
limits: Anecdotal. The authors' own tuning is a confound.
agent_relevance: Have the model write a generator or search procedure rather than a final object when the object can be scored.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Plan-and-Solve Prompting: math
finding: The prompt asks the model to devise a plan, then carry it out. It echoes Polya's plan-then-execute phases, though the paper does not cite Polya as its source.
numbers: text-davinci-003, zero-shot, six math sets. Zero-shot CoT average 70.4; PS+ average 76.7. GSM8K 56.4 to 59.3; SVAMP 69.9 to 75.7; AQuA 38.9 to 46.0. Of 46 wrong GSM8K answers: calculation 7%, missing step 12%, misunderstanding 27%.
limits: Table parsed from a garbled PDF layout; row assignment checked against the text (75.7 on SVAMP). Old model, greedy decoding. GSM8K gain is small.
agent_relevance: The plan step gives a few points on weaker models. It does not test Polya's 'look back'.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Plan-and-Solve: commonsense and symbolic
finding: Zero-shot PS+ beat zero-shot CoT on commonsense and symbolic tasks, but stayed below few-shot manual CoT on CSQA.
numbers: CSQA 71.9 vs 65.2 (few-shot CoT 78.3). StrategyQA 65.4 vs 63.8. Last Letter 75.2 vs 64.8 (few-shot 70.6). Coin Flip 99.6 vs 96.8.
limits: One model family; no significance tests.
agent_relevance: Planning prompts help on structured tasks and little on commonsense.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-Most Prompting
finding: Two stages: decompose into easier subproblems, then solve them in order using earlier answers. This is Polya's decomposing / auxiliary-problem heuristic made into a prompt.
numbers: SCAN with code-davinci-002: at least 99% in every split including length split using 14 exemplars, versus 16% for chain-of-thought. Specialised neural-symbolic models were trained on over 15,000 examples.
limits: SCAN is synthetic. Needs task-specific exemplars. Math word-problem gains were smaller.
agent_relevance: Decomposition into ordered subproblems is the best-supported Polya-type heuristic in LLM tests.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners
finding: The model first writes its own relevant example problems (and, for code, relevant knowledge), then solves the target. This is Polya's 'related solved problem' heuristic.
numbers: Average gain about +4% over baselines. Codeforces Acc@1: GPT-3.5-turbo 15% with the method vs GPT-4 16% with 3-shot CoT. Gain clearest on MATH, where fixed exemplars often mismatch the problem type.
limits: Table cells were garbled in text extraction, so per-cell GSM8K/MATH values are not recorded. Another subfield covers this paper in full.
agent_relevance: Self-made examples beat fixed ones when problem types vary. Check that self-made examples are correct (G2, G3).

source: Polymath project (Wikipedia)
finding: Polymath1 (Gowers, January 2009) on the density Hales-Jewett theorem had over 40 participants and was called 'probably solved' after about seven weeks. Papers appeared under D. H. J. Polymath, including a 2012 Annals paper.
numbers: Polymath8a bound H=4,680; Polymath8b H=246. Polymath5 (Erdos discrepancy) did not solve it; Tao solved it in 2015 after contributions from the project.
limits: No comment counts and no success rate across projects on the page.
agent_relevance: Open refinement of a proof works when many small contributions are checkable. Fits the multiplayer idea.

source: Polya (1954) Mathematics and Plausible Reasoning, and its link to Lakatos
finding: Polya's two volumes treat induction, analogy and patterns of plausible inference as how mathematicians guess before proving. Lakatos extended this from guessing to the later fate of a guess under counterexample.
numbers: Only dates and the dedication come from SEP. Bayesian forms of Polya's plausible-inference patterns are reported in later literature; not checked here.
limits: Book not opened. The Bayesian claim is from memory and unverified.
agent_relevance: Plausibility updates (a confirmed consequence raises credence, a verified rival lowers it) could be counted in code.

source: Philosophy of mathematical practice after Lakatos (lead only)
finding: A line of work (Hersh, Larvor and others) treats informal proof as the real object of study and formal proof as a later gloss. Not opened.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened; a lead for angles B and C, not a finding.
agent_relevance: Informal steps need checks that formal proof has built in; keep a step list that code can test.

source: Schoenfeld (1985): control and monitoring as the missing part
finding: Schoenfeld stressed that students must monitor their work and adjust tactics. Polya heuristics without control did not carry undergraduates through non-routine problems.
numbers: No sample sizes on the page; original video-coded numbers not read.
limits: Secondary summary only. Do not quote effect sizes from it.
agent_relevance: A progress limit that forces a switch is the code-side form of 'control' (impasse detector).

source: Polya heuristic list as machine operators (our mapping)
finding: The 12 named heuristics can be listed as operators: specialise, generalise, draw, analogy, auxiliary element, auxiliary problem, decompose, work backwards, vary the problem, induce, indirect proof, restate.
numbers: Pairs worth testing: specialise then generalise (conjecture refinement); vary the problem (finding hidden lemmas).
limits: Our mapping, not a study result.
agent_relevance: Candidate operator menu for the refine step; each operator can be scored by code on seeded items.

source: Davies et al. (2021): boundary of the method
finding: A model that cannot beat chance does not show that no pattern exists. A relation counts as found when accuracy is above chance on samples the model was not trained on.
numbers: Models train in several hours on one GPU. Data come from chosen distributions; regions can be picked to hunt for counterexamples.
quote: if the model cannot predict the relationship better than chance, it may mean that a pattern exists
limits: Limits are the authors' own text.
agent_relevance: A failed learnability probe is weak evidence; code must not use it to drop a conjecture.

source: Cross-paper synthesis: failure modes of AI conjecture work
finding: Across a10, a13, a14, a07: generators fail by triviality (true but dull), unchecked truth (non-trivial but maybe false), and scorer gaming.
numbers: LeanConjecturer: 3,776 of 12,289 non-trivial (31%). AlphaEvolve: leaky verifier. Ramanujan: digit match is not proof.
limits: Our synthesis, not a study.
agent_relevance: Three code filters: sharpening (Graffiti), independent hold-out (Davies), a closed formal or numeric check (Ramanujan, AlphaEvolve).
